requirement:
A language SHOULD include annotations in the owning item's structural hash
because they can affect the declaration's semantics. Each language defines
which attachments contribute to that hash. For example, a language that
includes a permission-checking decorator in a method's hash reflects the
addition of that decorator in both the method's own fingerprint and the
enclosing class's structural hash. The class's own fingerprint excludes
its methods under {cite}`requirements.references.structural_hash`.
rationale:
**Obligations.** The SHOULD in `requirements.sdk.outlines.attachments.fingerprint` has these testable parts. Each language that reports annotation attachments includes them in the owning item's structural hash. These are Rust attributes, Python decorators and TypeScript/TSX decorators. The other bundled languages report only comments. Adding or changing an annotation changes the item's own fingerprint. The same change alters the enclosing item's structural hash. The enclosing item's own fingerprint stays unchanged, per the cited `requirements.references.structural_hash`.

**Rust.**
- `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/tests.rs#fn[hashes_skip_whitespace_and_plain_comments_but_not_doc_comments]` changes `#[inline]` to `#[cold]` on `fn run`. It asserts that the node's structural hash changes. It also asserts that a plain comment between the attribute and the function does not change it.
- `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/tests.rs#fn[identity_hashes_include_own_attached_siblings_but_not_descendants]` edits or removes a child's `#[inline]` and doc comment inside `mod m`. The module's structural hash changes and its identity hash (the fingerprint) stays the same. The same test shows that an own attribute such as `#[cfg(test)]` changes an anonymous `use` node's identity hash. Both the attribute-present and attribute-absent cases are covered.

**Python.** `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/tests.rs#fn[python_decorators_attach_to_the_decorated_definition_for_hashing]` covers four cases.
- Changing `@cache` to `@other` changes `def[f]`'s hash.
- Removing the decorator changes `def[f]`'s hash. This is the converse of adding one.
- Blank-line changes between the decorator and `def` do not change the hash.
- A method decorator change alters the class's structural hash and leaves its identity hash unchanged. This is the exact scenario in the requirement's example.

**TypeScript and TSX.** `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/outline_content.rs#fn[typescript_and_tsx_decorators_belong_to_the_decorated_declaration]` runs for both `.ts` and `.tsx`. Changing `@trace` to `@logged` on a method changes the method's `fingerprint()`. It also changes the class's `structural_hash()` and leaves the class's `fingerprint()` unchanged. It also asserts the attachment records themselves.

**Bundled fingerprint test.** `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/outline_content.rs#fn[bundled_fingerprints_exclude_comments_and_preserve_word_boundaries]` covers the 64-hex fingerprint form and comment exclusion across languages. That behaviour belongs to `requirements.references.structural_hash`, not to the annotation obligation here.

**Gaps.** I found no gap. Each annotation-reporting language has a test for the item's own hash and for the ancestor's structural hash versus its fingerprint. Other attachment kinds (comments) are not annotations, so this requirement does not govern them.

text: :::{req} attachments.fingerprint
A language SHOULD include annotations in the owning item's structural hash
because they can affect the declaration's semantics. Each language defines
which attachments contribute to that hash. For example, a language that
includes a permission-checking decorator in a method's hash reflects the
addition of that decorator in both the method's own fingerprint and the
enclosing class's structural hash. The class's own fingerprint excludes
its methods under {cite}`requirements.references.structural_hash`.
:::{req} structural_hash
A node's structural hash MUST be the SHA-256 digest of an unambiguous encoding of
its outline-relevant structure, including siblings its profile attaches to it:
the kinds of its named grammar nodes and, in source order, its text pieces. A
text piece MUST be the text of a leaf token, or text inside a node that no child
token covers. Each text piece MUST be hashed as its ordered list of words, where
words are separated by whitespace, the whitespace itself, including leading and
trailing whitespace, is never hashed, and each word is encoded separately, so
`ab cd` and `abcd` differ. The same rule MUST apply in every language. Comments
MUST be excluded, except comment kinds the profile includes; the Rust profile MUST include doc comments. For an included comment, only its text and its
profile's comment group MUST be hashed, not its delimiter tokens such as `//`,
`///`, `//!`, `/*`, `*/`, or a leading `*`; the Rust profile's groups are inner
and outer doc comments. The words of consecutive included comments of one group
MUST be hashed as one ordered list, so reflowing them across more or fewer lines
or comments does not change the hash, while moving text between groups does. A `line`
node's hash MUST be computed by the same word rule over the line's text. A node's
identity hash MUST be computed the same way but MUST also exclude its outline
descendants and their attached siblings, so editing a descendant does not change
its ancestors' selectors.
:::{req} attachments
CSS reports only `Comment` attachments. These include `/* … */` blocks and
`//` line comments recognized by the bundled CSS grammar.
:::{req} attachments
Markdown reports only `Comment` attachments. Each HTML comment block whose
trimmed text starts with `<!--` and ends with `-->` is one attachment.
An inline HTML comment within a paragraph remains paragraph text, and
comment delimiters inside fenced code remain code.
:::{req} attachments
TOML reports only `Comment` attachments. Each `#` comment is one attachment,
including a comment following a value on the same line. A `#` inside a quoted
string belongs to the string.
:::{req} attachments
YAML reports only `Comment` attachments. Each `#` comment is one attachment,
including a comment following a mapping value. A `#` within quoted text or
within the content of a block scalar belongs to the scalar.
:::{req} attachments.comments
TypeScript and TSX report `//` line comments and `/* … */` block comments,
including `/** … */` documentation comments, as `Comment` attachments.
:::{req} attachments
Rust reports line and block comments, including outer and inner documentation
comments, as `Comment`. An outer attribute (`#[…]`) attached to an outline
item is an `Annotation` on that item. These are the two kinds Rust reports.
For example, a function preceded by `/// Verify the token.` and `#[inline]`
owns a `Comment` followed by an `Annotation`. A file-level `//!` comment
belongs to the file root.
:::{req} attachments
Python reports `#` comments as `Comment` and each decorator as one
`Annotation` on the decorated class or function. The decorator span starts
at `@` and includes the expression and any arguments. These are the two kinds
Python reports. Docstrings are string expressions.
